quote: Without the mark, a Spanish reader says BO-go-ta. The mark is part of the spelling, and the checker reads it like a Bogotano would.
problem: False stress in the stress lesson itself. By the rule three paragraphs up, a word ending in a vowel stresses the second-to-last syllable, so unaccented Bogota reads bo-GO-ta, never BO-go-ta. A learner who is trying to absorb the rule is told the opposite of what it predicts.
authority: Ortografia de la lengua espanola (RAE 2010), general accent rules; internal contradiction with the rule field of this script
replacement: Without the mark, a Spanish reader says bo-GO-ta, stress on the second-to-last syllable. The mark is part of the spelling, and the checker reads it like a Bogotano would.

quote: *ll* and *y* sound like the y in "yes".
problem: Y alone or word-final is a vowel. The learner has already met y (and), soy, muy, hay, and the Read and Pick line in this script contains Y Vale. The rule as written predicts "yeh" for and.
authority: Ortografia RAE 2010; RAE Nueva gramatica basica, sounds of y
replacement: *ll* and *y* sound like the y in "yes", but *y* alone or at the end of a word is a vowel: *y* (and) is "ee", and *soy* rhymes with "boy".

quote: One *r* is a quick tap; *rr*, or an *r* that starts a word, is rolled.
problem: Also rolled after n, l and s: Enrique, alrededor, Israel. Low stakes at this level, but the rule claims completeness and Enrique is a common name.
authority: RAE Ortografia 2010, letra r
replacement: One *r* is a quick tap; *rr*, or an *r* that starts a word or follows *n*, *l* or *s* (*Enrique*), is rolled.

quote:
A describing word matches the person or thing it describes: a man or a woman, one or more.

Words ending in *o* switch to *a* for a woman: *cansado*, *cansada*; *colombiano*, *colombiana*.
problem: First contact with agreement is framed entirely as sex (man or woman). Every example, Read and Pick, Your Turn and pitfall in the script is about people: 0 of the 28 examples and practice items agree with an inanimate noun. An English speaker leaves with "the a is for women", which undoes the gender lesson ("It's a label, not a meaning") and gives no model for la casa es pequena or el pan esta listo, la leche esta lista.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009), concordancia nominal; reasoning from the script g:gender-articles
replacement:
A describing word matches the noun it describes: masculine or feminine, one or more. With people that usually follows man or woman. With things it follows *el* or *la*: *el pan está listo*, *la leche está lista*.

Words ending in *o* switch to *a* for anything feminine: *cansado*, *cansada*; *colombiano*, *colombiana*.

quote: ¿Estás ocupada, Vale?
problem: None of the six examples shows agreement with a thing, though the title promises "people and things". Swap one in so the rule above is demonstrated.
authority: Reasoning from the script title and rule
replacement: El pan está listo y la leche está lista. = The bread is ready and the milk is ready.

quote: Teachers call this adjective agreement: an adjective agrees in gender and number with its noun.
problem: Here the learner writes es alta and esta cansada side by side, and the Personal task asks for both, yet the es/esta split with adjectives waits until g:ser-estar-adjectives in u15. For thirteen units the only guidance is the "lasting stuff" line in p:es-tiene-lleva. One sentence of the portrait/snapshot model now prevents the permanent/temporary folk rule from filling the gap.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, ser and estar chapter; the course own framing in x:ser-estar-adj (portrait or snapshot)
replacement: Teachers call this adjective agreement: an adjective agrees in gender and number with its noun. You'll notice *es alta* but *está cansada*: *es* says what someone is like, *está* how they are right now. That gets its own lesson later.

quote: Here you only need *me* and *te*; *le*, *nos* and *les* come later.
problem: Me gusta plus a named person commonly means attraction, and in Colombia it is read that way by default. The script drills it with no warning (readAndPick[0] Me gusta Tomas, [1] Te gusta Mariana), and the fix for liking someone as a person, me cae bien, arrives at u15 without mentioning the trap either. An English speaker will say Me gusta tu hermana to a friend and mean something innocent.
authority: Usage evidence; Butt and Benjamin on gustar with persons
replacement: Here you only need *me* and *te*; *le*, *nos* and *les* come later. One warning: about a person, *me gusta* usually means you're attracted to them. For things, places and activities it's always safe.

quote: ¿Te gusta Mariana?
problem: This and readAndPick[0] (Me gusta Tomas) model the crush reading as the neutral "like". Replace both with places or things that still test who pleases whom. A person is not needed to test direction.
authority: Usage evidence

quote: Two surprises this week: *el día* is masculine.
problem: The rule says -a is usually feminine and lists one exception. The large family in -ma (el problema, el idioma, el tema, el sistema, el programa, el clima) is never explained anywhere in the 916 scripts; a scan finds only the passing "a masculine noun like problema" in g:indefinites. La problema is the signature English-speaker error, and the node es for this very lesson contains la mano, which the script also never mentions.
authority: Nueva gramatica, genero de los sustantivos; corpus scan of all script rule, smallPrint and pitfall fields
replacement: Three surprises this week: *el día* is masculine, and so are many words in *-ma*, like *el problema* and *el idioma* (language). *La mano* (hand) is feminine despite its *-o*.

quote: Words in *-ante* or *-ente* don't change, so the article does the job: *el estudiante*, *la estudiante*.
problem: Mostly true, not absolute. La presidenta, la clienta and la dependienta are standard, and the course uses presidenta 24 times and clienta 6 times.
authority: RAE DPD s.v. presidente, cliente; corpus count
replacement: Most words in *-ante* or *-ente* don't change, so the article does the job: *el estudiante*, *la estudiante*.

quote: Grammar books call this grammatical gender. *El*/*la* are the definite articles; *un*/*una* are the indefinite articles.
problem: The rule gives -o masculine and -a feminine as the guess, with only día and agua as surprises. No script in the course names the -ma family (el problema, el idioma, el sistema, el tema, el programa) or la mano, la foto, la moto. These are high-frequency, and an English speaker who trusts the rule says la problema. The app relies on the article in each word card.
authority: Standard grammar; PCIC gramática 1.2
replacement: Grammar books call this grammatical gender. *El*/*la* are the definite articles; *un*/*una* are the indefinite articles. Watch for a few everyday breakers: *el problema*, *el idioma*, *el tema*, *el mapa*, *la mano*, *la foto*.

quote: For what you do in general, use the plain present: I'm working at a café these days is *Trabajo en un café*. Plans too: I'm going to Medellín tomorrow is *Mañana voy a Medellín*. Keep *estoy* plus *-ando* for right now, as you speak.
problem: The example is the classic case where the progressive is natural. "I'm working at a café these days" is exactly Estoy trabajando en un cafe, a temporary state of affairs; Latin American speakers use it freely. The learner is taught to reject good Spanish, and the course itself breaks the rule: u14-0056 Estoy aprendiendo espanol, por eso escribo mensajes largos; u08-0235 No estoy trabajando hoy.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, continuous forms (temporary or in-progress reading of vivo/estoy viviendo); Nueva gramatica, perifrasis de gerundio; usage evidence in the course bank
replacement: For what you do in general, use the plain present: I work at a café is *Trabajo en un café*. Plans too: I'm going to Medellín tomorrow is *Mañana voy a Medellín*. Keep *estoy* plus *-ando* for something in progress: right now, or going on around now for a while, like *Estoy aprendiendo español*.

quote: Ask yourself: is it happening at this very moment? If not, drop the *estoy*.
problem: Same over-narrow test as g:estar-gerund, stated as the decision rule for the whole contrast. It rejects Estoy leyendo un libro muy bueno said at lunch, or Estoy aprendiendo espanol. The real trap is habits, timetables and plans, which is what the English -ing wrongly invites.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, continuous forms; course bank u14-0056
replacement: Ask yourself: is it in progress around now, or is it a habit, a timetable or a plan? For a habit, a timetable or a plan, drop the *estoy*.

quote: The new ones are *le* and *les*, and they ignore gender: *le* is a man, a woman or *usted*. They are only ever for people.
problem: False as stated. Indirect objects are often things: A la sopa le falta sal, Le puse sal a la sopa, Le cambie el aceite al carro. The course itself teaches this in p:le-falta-sal and p:quedar-faltar-sobrar, so a later band has to undo the word "only". The same fact would also block the everyday ponle sal.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, complemento indirecto; course script p:le-falta-sal
replacement: The new ones are *le* and *les*, and they ignore gender: *le* is a man, a woman or *usted*. For now, use them for people.

quote: In front of the first verb is always safe: *¿Me estás…?*
problem: Not always. With hay que the pronoun cannot go in front (Hay que hacerlo, never Lo hay que hacer), and the same holds for me gusta verla and after a preposition (para verte). A learner told "always safe" will generalise. Corpus check: "lo/la hay que" occurs 0 times in scripts, story, scenes, bank and writing; "hay que" plus enclitic occurs 78 times.
authority: Nueva gramatica, subida de cliticos; corpus count across app/content
replacement: In front of *estás* is the safe spot here: *¿Me estás…?*

quote: Same meaning, both everyday Spanish.
problem: The rule says any verb plus infinitive gives a free choice. Hay que is a verb plus infinitive the learner has used since u03, and it allows only the glued position. Add the one exception they will actually hit.
authority: Nueva gramatica, subida de cliticos
replacement: Same meaning, both everyday Spanish. One exception you already know: *hay que* always glues it on: *Hay que hacerlo*.

quote: Gluing a word on moves the stress, so *escuchándote* needs its accent.
problem: Contradicts the rule in the same script ("add an accent to keep the stress where it was"). The stress does not move. The word grows, so the unchanged stress now falls three syllables from the end.
authority: Ortografia RAE 2010; internal contradiction
replacement: Gluing a word on doesn't move the stress. It now falls three syllables from the end, so *escuchándote* needs its accent.

quote: Siga derecho dos cuadras. Tome la TransMilenio. Pasen, sigan.
problem: Bogotanos say el TransMilenio or just TransMilenio, never la. The corpus has el TransMilenio 16 times, al TransMilenio 6, del TransMilenio 2, and la TransMilenio only here.
authority: Usage evidence, corpus count across app/content
replacement: Siga derecho dos cuadras. Tome el TransMilenio. Pasen, sigan.

quote: *-ar* verbs take *e*: *toma* becomes *tome*, *espera* becomes *espere*.
problem: As stated the rule produces *page from pagar and *busce from buscar. The script shows only cruzar, in a pitfall, yet bank u13-0680 has Pague en la caja. The spelling fix is already known from g:preterite-spelling-stem (pague, busque, empece), so one clause ties it together.
authority: Ortografia RAE 2010; course bank u13-0680
replacement: *-ar* verbs take *e*: *toma* becomes *tome*, *espera* becomes *espere*. Spelling keeps the sound, as in *pagué*: *pague*, *busque*, *cruce*.

quote: One that breaks the trick: *ir* gives *vaya*.
problem: Ser, saber, estar and dar also break it (sea, sepa, este, de). "One" invites building *soya or *esta from soy and estoy.
authority: Any reference conjugation; Nueva gramatica
replacement: The main one that breaks the trick: *ir* gives *vaya*.

quote: *Fue un desastre*: a description, so was.
problem: Calling fue "a description" collides with the next lesson, g:imperfect-states: "For describing, use *era*" and "*El sábado fue un desastre* sums up an event". The learner gets contradictory labels for the same sentence two units apart.
authority: Internal contradiction with g:imperfect-states rule; Nueva gramatica, aspecto perfectivo
replacement: *Fue un desastre*: it says what something was, so was.

quote: Teachers call this *estar* for location and states.
problem: The rule and its test ("if the answer is a place... reach for estar") have no exception, and the Your Turn line says "A place is a where, so it's está, not es." Events take ser, and the A1 bank uses this from u03: u03-0442 La fiesta es en el cafe o en el parque, u04-0356 La reunion fue en la oficina, u05-0933 La fiesta fue en casa de mi tio. The explicit contrast x:ser-event-estar-location waits until u17 d8.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, ser and estar with events; course bank
replacement: Teachers call this *estar* for location and states. One exception you'll meet soon: an event takes *es*, even with a place: *La fiesta es en el café*.

quote: And location is never *es*.
problem: Stated as an absolute and false for events, which the same unit range practises: u05-0933 La fiesta fue en casa de mi tio; u09-0691 Hoy el almuerzo es en casa de Gloria. A2 has to undo the word "never".
authority: Butt and Benjamin, ser and estar with events; course bank; x:ser-event-estar-location
replacement: And a place or a thing never takes *es* for where it is.

quote: Estoy aquí hace un rato.
problem: Tagged g:hace-ago, but this is hace with a present verb meaning "for" (duration). The script says the opposite: "the verb next to it is in the past", with the pitfall "Vale llega hace una hora" marked wrong. The duration use has its own node, g:hace-que-desde, at priority 220 in A2. The learner drills an unexplained counterexample to the rule of the week. Alternative fix: move the row to g:hace-que-desde.
authority: Internal contradiction with g:hace-ago rule and pitfalls[2]
replacement: Llegué hace un rato. = I got here a while ago.

quote: Estoy aquí hace un día y ya tengo problemas.
problem: Tagged g:hace-ago, but this is hace with a present verb meaning "for" (duration). The script says the opposite: "the verb next to it is in the past", with the pitfall "Vale llega hace una hora" marked wrong. The duration use has its own node, g:hace-que-desde, at priority 220 in A2. The learner drills an unexplained counterexample to the rule of the week. Alternative fix: move the row to g:hace-que-desde.
authority: Internal contradiction with g:hace-ago rule and pitfalls[2]
replacement: Llegué hace un día y ya tengo problemas. = I got here a day ago and I already have problems.

quote: Tomás vive aquí hace poco tiempo.
problem: Tagged g:hace-ago, but this is hace with a present verb meaning "for" (duration). The script says the opposite: "the verb next to it is in the past", with the pitfall "Vale llega hace una hora" marked wrong. The duration use has its own node, g:hace-que-desde, at priority 220 in A2. The learner drills an unexplained counterexample to the rule of the week. Alternative fix: move the row to g:hace-que-desde.
authority: Internal contradiction with g:hace-ago rule and pitfalls[2]
replacement: Tomás llegó aquí hace poco tiempo. = Tomás got here a short time ago.

quote: Tomás vive acá hace dos semanas.
problem: Tagged g:hace-ago, but this is hace with a present verb meaning "for" (duration). The script says the opposite: "the verb next to it is in the past", with the pitfall "Vale llega hace una hora" marked wrong. The duration use has its own node, g:hace-que-desde, at priority 220 in A2. The learner drills an unexplained counterexample to the rule of the week. Alternative fix: move the row to g:hace-que-desde.
authority: Internal contradiction with g:hace-ago rule and pitfalls[2]
replacement: Tomás llegó acá hace dos semanas. = Tomás got here two weeks ago.

quote: Llegué hace dos semanas. Mi abuela abrió el café hace cuarenta años.
problem: The story fixes the opening at 1978 and the app year at 2026: bank u06-0159 says hace cuarenta y ocho anos, and p:mas-de-number says mas de cuarenta. The en field needs the same change: forty-eight years ago.
authority: Internal consistency with bank u06-0159 and p:dates-years
replacement: Llegué hace dos semanas. Mi abuela abrió el café hace cuarenta y ocho años.

quote: A quick test: if English says good or bad, use *bueno* or *malo*. If English says well or badly, use *bien* or *mal*.
problem: The test fails on the commonest sentences: I feel bad is Me siento mal, That's good/fine is Esta bien, That's bad/wrong is Esta mal. The script's own card gives Estoy mal as "I'm not doing well", and u02-0314 uses esta mal for "wrong". The learner who follows the test produces me siento malo. The model should be what the word modifies, not what English says.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, adjectives and adverbs; course bank u02-0314
replacement: A quick test: if it describes a thing or a person, use *bueno* or *malo*. If it says how something is done, or how someone is doing, use *bien* or *mal*. So I feel bad is *Estoy mal*, even though English says bad.

quote: *Un* or *una* comes back only when you add something about the person, because then you're describing what kind: *Es un médico colombiano.*
problem: A learner will apply this to the job sentences they most need and produce Soy un profesor de ingles, Soy un ingeniero civil. Classifying additions keep the bare noun: Soy profesor de espanol (bank u01-0242, same unit), Es ingeniero civil, Es profesor universitario. The article returns with opinion or description: Es un medico muy bueno, Es un medico excelente.
authority: Nueva gramatica, articulo y atributos de ser; Butt and Benjamin, omission of the indefinite article; course bank u01-0242
replacement: *Un* or *una* comes back when you add an opinion or a description of the person: *Es un médico muy bueno.* Saying what kind of job keeps it bare: *Soy profesor de español.*

quote: Es médico colombiano.
problem: Marked wrong, but it is acceptable Spanish in the ordinary biographical frame (Es escritor colombiano, Es medico colombiano). The real error is the bare noun with an evaluative: Es medico muy bueno. Also accept Es ingeniero colombiano in yourTurn[6].
authority: Nueva gramatica, atributos sin determinante; usage evidence
replacement: {"wrong":"Es médico muy bueno.","right":"Es un médico muy bueno.","why":"With an opinion about him, *un* comes back."}

quote: No to: the verb follows straight on. Not *es difícil de aprender*.
problem: Over-broad. Es dificil de aprender is correct when "it" is the thing being learned: El ruso es dificil de aprender. The course says so later: u39-0263 Es dificil de aprender?, u39-0271 Este tema es dificil de explicar. The rule only applies when the verb has its own object, as the pitfall shows.
authority: Nueva gramatica, construcciones de infinitivo con adjetivos; Butt and Benjamin; course bank
replacement: No to: the verb follows straight on. Not *es difícil de aprender idiomas*.

quote: In Latin America you *tomar* the bus. *Coger* is the Spain word, and best avoided here.
problem: False for the course's own city. Coger is ordinary and clean in Colombia: coger el bus, coger un taxi, coger TransMilenio. It is rude in Mexico, Argentina and elsewhere, so tomar is a sound recommendation for neutral Spanish, but the reason given is wrong and Cojo el bus should not be presented as an error a Bogotano would hear as foreign.
authority: Usage evidence, Colombian Spanish; DLE s.v. coger
replacement: *Tomar* works everywhere. Colombians say *coger* too, but in Mexico and Argentina it's a rude word, so *tomo el bus* is the safe habit.

quote: In Latin America you *tomar* the bus. *Coger* is the Spain word, and best avoided here.
problem: Same point. Cojo el bus en la 72 is normal Bogotá Spanish, and it is listed as wrong.
authority: Diccionario de americanismos (ASALE); usage evidence
replacement: Across Latin America you can always *tomar* the bus. *Coger* is fine in Colombia but vulgar in Mexico and Argentina, so *tomar* is the safe choice.

quote: Questions don't swap the words round the way English does. *¿Eres de Bogotá?* is the statement with question marks, and the first one is upside down.
problem: True only as an option for yes/no questions. Spanish does invert: the same script accepts Es usted de Cali, g:present-ar readAndPick[8] is Trabaja usted en Bogota, and p:question-word-order requires the verb before the subject (Donde vive Vale). The first lesson plants a blanket claim the learner must unlearn in the next unit.
authority: Nueva gramatica, orden de palabras en interrogativas; internal contradiction with p:question-word-order
replacement: A yes-or-no question doesn't have to swap any words round. *¿Eres de Bogotá?* is the statement with question marks, and the first one is upside down.

quote: *deber*: should, the advice word. *Debes ir al médico.*
problem: Glossed as a pure "should", then in the next paragraph no debes is "mustn't", which is stronger than the positive. The bank uses it for all of them: u09-0439 No debo comer pan = shouldn't, u10-0908 debo pagar = have to, u10-1118 Debemos cerrar = have to. Deber expresses duty; the softer "should" of advice properly belongs to deberias, which comes later.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, deber; Nueva gramatica, perifrasis modales; course bank
replacement: *deber*: must or should, what's the right thing to do. *Debes ir al médico.*

quote: *No debes venir* means you mustn't come.
problem: See the deber gloss above. The trap with no tienes que stays intact if the gloss admits both strengths, and it matches bank u09-0439.
authority: Course bank u09-0439
replacement: *No debes venir* means you mustn't come, or you shouldn't.

quote: *deber*: should, the advice word. *Debes ir al médico.*
problem: x:tener-que-deber later teaches debo as must and deberías as should. In the same script the pitfall glosses no debes as "you mustn't". English speakers map must and should firmly, so one form with two glosses across the course leaves them guessing.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish ch. 21
replacement: *deber*: must or should, the duty word. *Debes ir al médico.*

quote:
*lo*: him, or it for an *el* word (*el contrato*)
*la*: her, or it for a *la* word (*la cuenta*)
*los*: them (men, mixed groups, *los* words)
*las*: them (women, *las* words)
problem: Omits lo/la/los/las as "you" for usted and ustedes. The only statement in the whole course is at B1 (p:perdona-que-interrumpa), yet A1 uses it: bank u13-0701 Esperen un momento, ya los atiendo, and the chunk Que pena molestarlo. In a course where usted is everywhere this is the reading a learner most needs and cannot derive.
authority: Nueva gramatica, pronombres atonos de cortesia; course bank
replacement:
*lo*: him, you (a man you call *usted*), or it for an *el* word (*el contrato*)
*la*: her, you (a woman you call *usted*), or it for a *la* word (*la cuenta*)
*los*: them or you all (men, mixed groups, *los* words)
*las*: them or you all (women, *las* words)

quote: Some Spanish verbs travel with a little word that points back at whoever is doing them.
problem: No reusable model. The title and node promise me levanto, te duchas, se acuesta, but no example or practice item uses them; the rule says "You'll get those verbs later this week". What is drilled is irse, sentirse, encontrarse, parecerse, none of which shows the core idea that the action comes back on the doer. The contrast that creates the model (lavo el carro / me lavo; acuesto al nino / me acuesto) never appears, nor voy versus me voy. The learner gets "some verbs have a little word". Needs a rewrite so the first examples are true reflexives with a non-reflexive partner, which means introducing lavar, levantar or similar before this script.
authority: Nueva gramatica, verbos pronominales; Butt and Benjamin, pronominal verbs

quote: La carta se trata de la casa.
problem: Tratarse de is impersonal and takes no subject in the standard: La carta trata de la casa, or Se trata de la casa. La carta se trata de is widespread in casual speech but the Academy rejects it, and a learner should not be taught it as the model. Same defect at u49-t-verbs-prepositions-0003 (outside this band).
authority: RAE DPD s.v. tratar(se)
replacement: Se trata de la casa. = It's about the house.

quote: Simón cayó de la silla y ahora no habla.
problem: In speech an accidental fall is caerse. Bare cayo reads as journalistic or literary here, and for a person it sounds wrong in a conversational sentence. Natural Spanish beats the lexeme tag: the learner already has se from u09.
authority: Usage evidence; Butt and Benjamin, caer and caerse
replacement: Simón se cayó de la silla y ahora no habla. = Simón fell off the chair and now he isn't talking.

quote: Mi abuela cayó en la calle, pero está bien.
problem: In speech an accidental fall is caerse. Bare cayo reads as journalistic or literary here, and for a person it sounds wrong in a conversational sentence. Natural Spanish beats the lexeme tag: the learner already has se from u09.
authority: Usage evidence; Butt and Benjamin, caer and caerse
replacement: Mi abuela se cayó en la calle, pero está bien. = My grandmother fell in the street, but she's OK.

quote: El pan cayó al piso.
problem: In speech an accidental fall is caerse. Bare cayo reads as journalistic or literary here, and for a person it sounds wrong in a conversational sentence. Natural Spanish beats the lexeme tag: the learner already has se from u09.
authority: Usage evidence; Butt and Benjamin, caer and caerse
replacement: El pan se cayó al piso. = The bread fell on the floor.

quote: El celular cayó en el café.
problem: In speech an accidental fall is caerse. Bare cayo reads as journalistic or literary here, and for a person it sounds wrong in a conversational sentence. Natural Spanish beats the lexeme tag: the learner already has se from u09.
authority: Usage evidence; Butt and Benjamin, caer and caerse
replacement: El celular se cayó en el café. = The phone fell into the coffee.

quote: Pido una limonada, pero prefiero el aguapanela.
problem: Aguapanela is stressed on the penultimate, so its initial a is unstressed and it takes la, as p:el-agua-fria explains with arepa. Every other occurrence in the course (bank u10, u15, story ch039, the lexeme entry) has la or una aguapanela. A learner could reasonably overgeneralise from el agua.
authority: Nueva gramatica, el ante a tonica; RAE DPD s.v. el; course corpus
replacement: Pido una limonada, pero prefiero la aguapanela.
